notes.meaning: John the Baptist makes it clear that the Messiah who comes after him in time is far higher in rank and dignity. Loosening sandal straps was viewed as a dirty, menial task reserved only for household slaves, and Jewish rabbis taught that even disciples should never be asked to do it. John felt completely unworthy to perform even this lowest service for Jesus.

These events took place across the Jordan River at a village named Bethany. This was an eastern river crossing, not the Bethany near Jerusalem where Mary, Martha, and Lazarus lived. Because crowds frequently crossed the river here, John gave his public witness where many people could hear.

John sees Jesus walking toward him and points Him out as the Lamb chosen by God. In the Old Testament, lambs were sacrificed during Passover and every morning and evening at the temple to pay for sin, which means wrongdoing against God. Jesus came as the final sacrifice who willingly bears the guilt of sinners and carries it away.

differ.view: Wesley taught that Christ atoned for all the sins of all mankind, meaning that the reach of sin and the world are of equal extent.
Calvinists teach that 'the world' means Christ's saving work is not limited to ethnic Israel, but effectively cleanses believers from every nation.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching connects the Lamb of God directly to the Passover sacrifice and the celebration of the Eucharist, seeing Jesus offered as the new Passover feast.

notes.meaning: John explains that Jesus is the very person he had been announcing to the crowds. Although Jesus began His public work after John, He holds a far higher place because He existed from all eternity before John was ever born. John is merely a herald preparing the road for the eternal King.

John explains that he did not personally recognize Jesus as the Messiah before this time. The two men had grown up in different regions—Jesus in the town of Nazareth and John in the desert—preventing any plot to stage a fake appearance. God sent John to baptize with water so that the true Messiah could be openly introduced to the people of Israel.

John describes what he saw with his own eyes when he baptized Jesus in the river. God's Holy Spirit came down from heaven in the gentle form of a dove and remained upon Him. In earlier times, the Spirit would visit prophets or kings for special tasks, but on Jesus the Holy Spirit rested permanently.

God gave John a clear sign ahead of time so he would recognize the Christ without any mistake. The Lord told John that the One on whom the Spirit rested would be the One who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. While John's baptism used water as an outward picture of repentance, Jesus gives the inward gift of the Holy Spirit to cleanse hearts and grant new life.

Because John saw the heavenly sign and heard God's confirmation at the river, he gave an open testimony. He told the gathered crowds that Jesus is truly the divine Son of God. His purpose as a prophet was fulfilled by pointing everyone away from himself and toward Jesus.

The following day, John was standing at his regular place along the Jordan with two of his followers. One follower was Andrew, and the other was likely John, who wrote this Gospel and humbly left his own name out. Even after preaching to large crowds, John spent careful time teaching this small circle of disciples.

As Jesus walked past, John fixed his eyes on Him and repeated his joyful message: 'Look, the Lamb of God!' John had no desire to build a personal following or keep his students to himself. By speaking these words again, he gently encouraged his disciples to leave him and follow Jesus.

Hearing their teacher's announcement, the two disciples immediately left John and started walking after Jesus. They trusted John's word that Jesus was the promised Savior who takes away sin. Their action shows that a true believer is always ready to follow Christ above any human teacher.

Jesus heard their footsteps, turned around, and asked them, 'What do you want?' He was not trying to turn them away, but was kindly inviting them to speak their minds. Addressing Him as 'Rabbi,' which means Teacher, they asked where He was staying so they could talk privately with Him without being rushed.

Jesus warmly welcomed them by saying, 'Come and see.' They went along with Him to His lodging and stayed with Him for the rest of the day, since it was already late afternoon, around four o'clock. This quiet evening spent with Jesus became a life-changing turning point for both men.

One of the two men who followed Jesus after hearing John's words was Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter. The writer of the Gospel leaves himself unnamed out of modesty, though he remembered every detail of that first meeting. Andrew is introduced through his well-known brother, whom he was eager to bring along.

The first thing Andrew did after spending time with Jesus was search for his brother Simon. He joyfully announced that they had found the Messiah, which is the Hebrew word for the Christ, meaning God's Anointed King. When someone discovers the good news of Jesus, their first instinct is to share it with the people they love.

Andrew brought Simon to meet Jesus, who looked closely at him and spoke his name and family background. Jesus then gave him the new name 'Cephas' in Aramaic, translated as 'Peter' in Greek, which means a stone or rock. Although Peter was often quick-tempered and unsteady, Jesus knew the solid church leader he would become through God's grace.

The next day, Jesus decided to travel north to the region of Galilee. He sought out Philip and gave him a clear and direct command: 'Follow Me.' This was the first time Jesus formally called someone to join Him as a full-time disciple.

Philip was from Bethsaida, a fishing town situated on the northern coast of the Sea of Galilee. Andrew and Peter also grew up in this same village before later settling in nearby Capernaum. Coming from the same neighborhood made it likely that these men already knew one another and had shared their hopes for the Messiah.

Philip promptly went to find his friend Nathanael to share the wonderful discovery. He told him they had found the Savior described long ago by Moses in the Law and predicted by the prophets. Philip called Him Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph, using the common name people in the region used for Jesus' earthly household.

Nathanael was doubtful and asked whether anything good could come from a small, insignificant town like Nazareth. The village was not mentioned in the Old Testament and carried a poor reputation among neighboring Galileans. Instead of arguing about hometown rivalries, Philip offered the simplest test: 'Come and see' for yourself.

As Nathanael approached, Jesus commended him as a true Israelite who had no dishonesty or deceit in him. This statement stood in sharp contrast to Jacob, the forefather of Israel, who had used trickery before God renamed him Israel. Nathanael was an honest and sincere man who was ready to receive the truth with an open heart.

Nathanael was surprised that a stranger could know his inner character and asked Jesus how He knew him. Jesus told him that He had seen him under the fig tree before Philip ever spoke to him. Sitting under a fig tree was a common place for private prayer and meditation, and Nathanael recognized that Jesus possessed supernatural knowledge of his secret life.

Nathanael laid aside all his earlier doubts and made a heartfelt confession of faith. He called Jesus 'Rabbi' and declared Him to be both the 'Son of God' and the 'King of Israel.' With these words, he confessed both who Jesus is in His divine person and what He came to do as the promised ruler of God's people.

Jesus asked if Nathanael believed simply because of what was revealed about the fig tree, welcoming his quick faith with pleasure. He then promised that Nathanael and the other followers would see far greater evidence than this initial sign. Their trust would soon be strengthened by the wonders and teachings of Jesus' ministry.

Jesus added the solemn phrase 'Truly, truly,' promising that they would all see heaven open and God's angels going up and down on the Son of Man. This recalls Jacob's dream of a ladder stretching between earth and heaven. Jesus Himself is that living connection, bringing the presence, power, and salvation of God down to the human race.
